newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower in US, eyes Japan/US trade data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower in US, eyes Japan/US trade data.

text.p: The dollar garnered little direction from assorted U.S. economic data, ending slightly lower in advance of Japanese and U.S. trade numbers and a gathering of leaders from the major economies later this week.

The dollar drifted off in very light trade, after opening near its overnight highs. The yen got some support as the market braced for the release of May data on Japanese trade early on Wednesday, traders said.
Meanwhile, U.S. reports on Tuesday showed the economy continued to grow at a healthy -- although somewhat more subdued -- clip in May.

But dealers said signs are few that growth is creating enough inflation to prompt speculation the dollar might soon get support from a change in Federal Reserve policy to higher, from steady interest rates.

"It's just the sort of thing to keep the Fed happy," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan in New York. "We were not too excited one way or the other -- the big focus is on tonight's Japanese trade numbers and on Thursday's U.S. numbers."
The dollar ended at 1.7305/10 marks, off from 1.7356/61 at the open and 113.28/33 yen, off from 113.60/70.
A tame 0.1 percent rise in the May Consumer Price Index led the string of releases. The core rate rose 0.2 percent. The market was looking for a 0.2 percent rise in both.
Other data showed a 4.8 percent fall in housing starts and a somewhat robust 0.4 percent rise in industrial output in May.

The Japanese trade numbers seem to be taking on added weight this time around. They will immediately precede Thursday's Commerce Department report on the April U.S. trade deficit and the three-day gathering of leaders from the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations in Denver starting Friday.

"We had a big ... jump in Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. last month and that's really kind of added some urgency to (Treasury Secretary Robert) Rubin asking for Japan to address its external balance," said Keith Woodfin, an analyst at consulting firm Foreign Exchange Analytics.
President Clinton is expected to zero in on Japan's trade surplus when he sits down with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Denver, a U.S. Treasury official said on Tuesday.
Economists expect Japan's surplus, to rise to 548.5 billion yen in May, from 229 billion a year earlier. Forecasts ranged from 400 billion yen to 760 billion yen.

"Dollar/yen got pushed down on the note that came out that Clinton and Hashimoto would have a one-on-one meeting at which it was expected Clinton would use the opportunity to stress Japan should not allow their trade surplus to rise substantially," Pettit said.
Elsewhere, the dollar erased an early rally against the Swiss franc, falling to 1.4445/55 Swiss from 1.4475/85.
"We came off the highs again, with offers above 1.4500 in dollar/Swiss and the fear of that 1.74 level again in dollar/mark," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
The dollar was little changed at Canadian $1.3862/67, compared to C$1.3860/65.
The pound rose to $1.6392/02 from $1.6380/90 and the Australian dollar rose to $0.7508/13 from $0.7478/83.
